turns.text: When my supervisor asks for an update, I freeze. I worry that asking for more time will sound like I am avoiding the work.

Could we draft one sentence asking for a little more time? We could write it or practise saying it; which would be more useful to you?

Then we will write, and leave speaking practice aside. You choose the extra time you need and write one sentence; I will help check that the request is clear.

turns.text: At bedtime I worry about missing my morning train and about a repair bill that has not arrived. Both feel as though I must deal with them tonight, and I feel overwhelmed.
The two worries feel equally urgent tonight, even though the bill is not here yet. Feeling overwhelmed makes sense when both seem to demand an answer at once.
Could we sort these worries into what I can do tonight and what must wait until tomorrow? I would like to put the two groups in a short note.

Yes, let us make that two-group note. Put one action you can take tonight in the first group, and the worry that must wait in the second; I will help if a group is unclear. This keeps the train preparation separate from the bill you cannot check tonight.
My note says: Tonight, set the alarm. Tomorrow, ask about the repair bill. Putting them in two groups helps me see what I can leave until tomorrow.
We will keep your two groups as written and finish this note here.

turns.text: I look forward to talking with my friend, but our calls run through my reading time. I feel torn about ending them.
It sounds as though you are angry with your friend and want to stop these calls.
No, I am not angry and I do not want to stop talking. I want a way to end a call kindly when I need to read.

I got that wrong: you value these calls and want to protect your reading time, not stop talking to your friend. Wanting a limit does not mean you care less. Could we try saying one short closing sentence?
Yes, let us try a closing sentence. I will say: I have enjoyed talking, and I am going to read now. The words fit what I need, but saying them aloud feels awkward.
We can slow the sentence down and stop after the first part. You do not need to say the whole line at once.
